rv.q: For all its antiquated but well meaning attitudes – it’s a warm tribute to the author.

Indian Ink has deep notes of grief and love, which Jonathan Kent’s production sounds perfectly from a cast in which Gavi Singh Chera is powerful as Das, who can love an Englishwoman but not the British.
This play feels too much like an artful formal experiment to be truly great.
Kent’s pleasing revival may serve as an appetizer for his modern classic, Arcadia, opening at the Old Vic next month.
Still, this remains one for Stoppard completists only.
Jonathan Kent’s production doesn’t get around the problems that, despite moving moments, remain in the bones of the play.
The debates may anticipate today's culture wars, but they now feel dated and lack the intellectual pyrotechnics that mark Stoppard's finest work.
Starring the ever-green Felicity Kendall, it’s a tremendously entertaining, enthralling and evocative play.
Timing has made something quietly momentous out of Indian Ink, a once-trifling Tom Stoppard play that has a mesmeric power in Jonathan Kent’s deeply felt Hampstead Theatre revival.
The result is a gentle, amusing and often surprising gem of a play and a fitting tribute to the great man himself who was undoubtedly smiling down on opening night.
This revival of Indian Ink was always likely to be emotional.
This is not Stoppard’s greatest play, but still a good one, and this production, especially in its final scene, is a fine and fitting remembrance as it looks back on his fictional poet’s life.
It’s still a radio play to me, like much of Stoppard’s work, sui generis creations that reward listening and are bursting to share the knowledge he has dug up.

While the loss of Tom Stoppard is still fresh in the hearts and minds of fans and theatregoers, this new production at Hampstead Theatre shows that his ideas are still universal, his themes still prescient, and his work still able to evoke genuine emotion in an audience.
This is a play that enthralls while keeping its audience behind carefully constructed barriers.

cn.t: This Stoppard revival gains poignant resonance following the playwright's recent death, particularly with Kendal's involvement, but critics find the play itself a "second-rank" work whose themes feel dated despite elegant staging.
